paragraphs.atlas-postgres.abstract|172a8d72776b3814: In a Compose install the image is built in the repo from `deploy/postgres/Dockerfile`: the official `postgres:16-trixie` (pinned tag and digest, followed by Dependabot) with its `gosu` Go binary replaced by a small `setpriv` shell shim, which removes the image's only fixable critical vulnerability without changing the entrypoint, PGDATA or the Postgres binaries. The OSS stack builds the same change on the pgvector image (`deploy/postgres/pgvector.Dockerfile`). An image swap is done with a verified backup first, then `tools/db_collation_check.sh` after the restart; a `REINDEX` is needed only when it reports a collation mismatch (a glibc change underneath the volume). On OpenShift the database is a CloudNativePG Cluster (`deploy/openshift/components/cnpg/`) running the operator's PostgreSQL 16 image, and an image change goes through the Cluster spec.
paragraphs.atlas-postgres.abstract|60794f37efc638bb: In a Compose install, what persists across a container recreate is exactly the `atlas-pgdata` named volume; removing that volume is a full data reset (on OpenShift, the CNPG Cluster's persistent volumes). No Alembic, by decision: `atlas-migrate upgrade` runs startup's schema steps (`create_all` plus the additive `_reconcile_graph_schema`) and exits; see `atlas-postgres-migrations`. Backup is opt-in: the product's backup service is `atlas-backup` on Compose, and the `cnpg-objectstore-plugin` component on OpenShift; until one is enabled there is no backup, and an install that chooses none should record that as an intent.
paragraphs.atlas-postgres.detail|fda82ae8d8d68cda: The gotcha worth knowing: `create_all()` on an EMPTY database never exercises the `ALTER TABLE` reconcile path, so a schema change verified only against a fresh database has not verified the path a populated deploy actually takes. Verify against a populated staging database before merging anything schema-shaped.
paragraphs.atlas-postgres:docs/nodes/atlas-postgres:
The database's storage is the only thing that survives a container recreate — in the Compose install the
`atlas-pgdata` named volume (recreating the `atlas-postgres` container without removing the volume
preserves all data; removing the volume is a full reset), on OpenShift the CloudNativePG cluster's
volumes — and there is **no startup ingest to re-populate it from**. Boot reads no file and never overwrites graph data. What it does write is schema-shaped: the `node_type` and `edge_type` registries and the `task_id_seq` floor, every boot; on an empty graph, the seed the install's `ATLAS_SEED` profile names (`none`, `demo` or `self`; the code default, `homelab`, is a personal tree), plus the system node. So losing this storage loses the graph, and it comes back only from the install's backups: the `atlas-backup` loop in the Compose install, the CloudNativePG backup component on OpenShift.
paragraphs.atlas-retrieval.abstract|575dd696570257f: `atlas-retrieval` is the **optional** semantic half of "tell me about X" (ADR 0044). It keeps a vector index of what Atlas already holds — one *card* per world node (name, type, summary, abstract, detail) and the **served** documents of those nodes, split on headings — and answers searches with it, so a question asked in someone's own words, or in Swedish about something documented in English, finds its starting points. The index lives in Atlas' own Postgres (pgvector), never in another service, and every row of it is derived: it can be dropped and rebuilt at any time.
paragraphs.atlas-retrieval.abstract|b712621a0a1391a: Code: `backend/retrieval/` (`query.py` is the query side). Measuring recall against full text, and whether `hybrid` should ever become a default, is an open measurement (ADR 0044, Verification).
paragraphs.atlas-retrieval.detail|bd1b6dc86730284c: **The embedder is configuration, never code.** Any OpenAI-compatible `/embeddings` endpoint: a local model behind an OpenAI-compatible model proxy on the same server, or a hosted deployment elsewhere. `https://` is required except to loopback, and certificate verification cannot be switched off (`ATLAS_EMBED_CA_BUNDLE` names a private CA instead). The key is read from a FILE on every call, so a rotated key needs no restart; a key in a plain environment variable is refused. For Azure OpenAI there is the `api-key` header, and `entra` mode: an Entra ID token from the workload or managed identity the process runs as, cached and refreshed before it expires, with no key at all.
paragraphs.atlas-retrieval:docs/nodes/atlas-retriev:
The add-on has two halves that never call each other: the **write path** of the graph, which is
untouched, and the **reconciler**, which reads the graph and keeps the derived index in step.
The query side reads the index and re-checks visibility and doc
serving against `node` at query time, so a lagging index is stale, never wrong.

The image swap keeps the data directory (same major, same format), but the **Debian release
must match the one the volume was initialised under**: a glibc change underneath a live data
directory can change collation order, and text indexes then disagree with the data. The plain
`pgvector/pgvector:*-pg16` tag is Debian 12 (glibc 2.36); the image Atlas builds, like the
CloudNativePG `standard-trixie` image the OpenShift install uses, is Debian 13 (glibc 2.41). That is
why the Compose install builds the trixie Dockerfile and not the upstream tag. After any swap on a
Compose install, run `bash tools/db_collation_check.sh "$(docker compose ps -q atlas-postgres)"`
(SECURITY.md).

- **OSS Compose install**: add the overlay `deploy/oss/retrieval.yml` (atlas-api joins `egress`;
  the key is the compose secret `embed_key`), and set the "Retrieval" block of `.env.example`. The
  base install already builds its Postgres image from `deploy/postgres/pgvector.Dockerfile` —
  pgvector on postgres:16, **Debian 13**, gosu replaced.
- **OpenShift**: the `retrieval` component, which also has the CloudNativePG operator create the
  `vector` extension from the `Database` object; keep a `standard` PostgreSQL image, since `minimal`
  has no pgvector (`deploy/openshift/README.md`).
- **Hosted provider** (Azure AI Foundry / Azure OpenAI): the deployment URL as given, and either
  `ATLAS_EMBED_AUTH_HEADER=api-key` with the key in the file, or `entra` with no key.
- **A separate embedding node**: its https URL; `ATLAS_EMBED_CA_BUNDLE` if its certificate is
  from a private CA.

Example of a self-hosted setup: the embedder is a model proxy's `bge-m3` route (1024 dimensions,
multilingual, no prefixes), served by an embedding server on the server's own GPU. atlas-api reaches
the proxy over TLS at `https://llm.example.internal:4443/v1`, a TLS front in front of the proxy.
Scope `all`: the endpoint is on the server itself and no text leaves it (ADR 0044, "Also decided").
The key is the proxy's key, as a file (e.g. `<secrets-dir>/embed_key`); rotate it there and in the
proxy together.

Write the new key to the key file. It is read on every call, so no restart is needed. The
endpoint must accept the new key first; rotate the endpoint's key and the file together. A wrong
key shows as `degraded: embedder at <host> answered 400` (a model proxy without a database may
answer a wrong key with 400 "No connected db", not 401).

To turn it off: set `ATLAS_RETRIEVAL=off` and recreate `atlas-api` the same way (in Compose, from
`docker-compose.yml` alone). The two tables stay behind and nothing reads them; dropping them is
optional and loses only derived data.

Stop the embedder (the embedding server behind the endpoint). The next pass reports `degraded: …`, the
index stays as it was, and search keeps answering in full text. Start it again; the next pass
returns to `on`.

`/api/health` carries the same `state` as `retrieval`. Without a token, the atlas-api container's
log (`docker logs <atlas-api>`, or `oc logs deployment/atlas-api` on OpenShift) shows the boot line
(`retrieval add-on on: …` or `… unavailable: <reason>`), and an owner's
`GET /api/retrieval/status` shows how many sources and chunks are indexed or still pending.

It is configuration, not a service. In a Docker Compose install it is the Retrieval block of
the install's `.env` plus the `retrieval.yml` overlay, which gives `atlas-api` its egress route and
the key file; every later `docker compose` command must name both files
(`-f docker-compose.yml -f retrieval.yml`, or set `COMPOSE_FILE`), or `atlas-api` goes back to the
base file. On OpenShift the same switch and the embeddings egress come from the install's
overlay (a `retrieval` kustomize component is planned for this), applied with the install's own
deploy procedure.
Per stack, in the order test (the fork) → staging → live, each with the owner's go:

All of this is owner-only. Run the curl calls on the server against `localhost:8095` with a
token from a file (`curl -K`), never a token on the command line.

1. The TLS front for the embedding endpoint is up (e.g. `https://llm.example.internal:4443`).
2. Fill in the Retrieval block of the install's configuration (`ATLAS_RETRIEVAL=on`, the URL, model
   and dimension) and write the endpoint's key to the embed key file (e.g. `<secrets-dir>/embed_key`,
   never printed). Check it: `docker compose --profile retrieval run --rm atlas-retrieval`.
3. Restart with the install's own deploy procedure, a staging environment first if the install has
   one: in Compose `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f retrieval.yml up -d`. The database needs
   pgvector: atlas-postgres is built from `deploy/postgres/pgvector.Dockerfile` (Debian 13, the same
   glibc as the default image), and the data directory carries over.
4. Verify: if the Postgres image changed, the collation check must be clean (a glibc change can
   corrupt text indexes; a finding stops the rollout), the boot line must say `on`, and the index
   must fill (`GET /api/retrieval/status`).
5. Once per environment: stop the embedding server, see `degraded`, start it again.
paragraphs.atlas-security.abstract|6568a8c78aeb6c8e: **The boundary against `atlas-ingress`**, its sibling under `atlas`: ingress is *the path in* — routing, TLS termination, tunnels, hostnames, what is exposed at all. Security is the policy applied once a request has arrived. The two meet in exactly one place worth remembering: the session cookie is `__Host-` prefixed and therefore `Secure`, and `Secure` cookies never travel over plain HTTP — so a login cannot succeed without a certificate. That is an ingress fact with a security cause, and it is why an install reached on its LAN needs a reverse proxy with a certificate in front of it.
paragraphs.atlas-security.abstract|9ffce144b5d43105:
- **Deny by default at one gate.** `AuthGate` is ASGI middleware, not route-level `Depends`, so it covers every route, every mount and every path that does not exist — including a route added six months from now. `/api/health` is deliberately not on the public exempt list.
- **The exempt list is short, pinned, and reviewed by a failing test.** `PUBLIC_ROUTES` in `backend/auth.py` is the whole of what the gate does not refuse; `verify_object_graph.py` asserts it equals an exact frozenset, so an addition cannot land without someone editing the assertion, and the convention is that an addition carries an ADR note. Two entries are there because a page you can only read *after* signing in is not available to the person deciding whether to sign in: `/auth/privacy` (ADR-less, older than the ADR convention) and — since 2026-08-25, ADR 0035 — **`/`, the bare domain**, which now serves a public description of the product instead of the login form. Three opt-in settings extend it with exact paths, never a prefix: the OIDC start and callback routes (`ATLAS_AUTH_PROVIDERS`, ADR 0041), the handbook (`ATLAS_PUBLIC_DOCS=1`, ADR 0047) and the landing site's files (`ATLAS_LANDING=v2`, ADR 0049); unset, the list is exactly the one above.
- **A public route is not the same as a fixed response.** `/` reads `auth.current_principal` in its own handler and redirects a signed-in browser to `/board`; the gate is what does not refuse it, and the handler is what decides what it says. `/board` itself was NOT made public, and neither was anything under `/assets/*` — measured on the live hosts on the day it shipped, because a login gate that fails for a path *prefix* is the shape of this project's two worst near-misses.
- **Fail closed at boot.** The peppers and the origin allow-list raise at *import*, before uvicorn binds. There is no `ATLAS_AUTH_DISABLED` and no bootstrap account.
- **One write guard.** `auth.guard_write` is the only answer to "may this request change data", and — since 2026-08-15 — it enforces the caller's scope on top of authenticating them, fail-closed for any route it has no scope mapping for.
paragraphs.atlas-security.detail|ff6a06d14934819b: **Scope enforcement closed the one gap that mattered here.** Until 2026-08-15 a service token's scopes were recorded and displayed but never checked; that is fixed — every mutating route now maps to a required scope and refuses a caller who does not carry it. The remaining discipline is choosing what scope to mint, not hoping nothing checks it.
paragraphs.atlas-security:docs/nodes/atlas-security:
- **A Bearer session (the common agent path) is never scope-checked for CSRF and never redirected
  to a login page** — an invalid or missing Bearer credential is always `401` JSON, even on a
  route that would `302` for a browser, specifically so a script never parses an HTML login page
  as data.
- **A hidden node and a nonexistent one return the SAME 404**, deliberately: a distinguishable
  refusal confirms a guessed id. So grant drift presents as *"the MCP says that node does not
  exist"* rather than as a permission error — check grants before believing a 404.
- **`must_change_password` is re-read from `auth_user` on every request, never cached on the
  session row** — a stale cached `false` would be a bypass with no revocation path. A principal
  stuck in that state reaches almost nothing: `MUST_CHANGE_ALLOWLIST` is a handful of paths, and
  everything else is `302`/`403` until the password is changed.
- **ADR 0026 — the decision `_visible_node_ids` says it applies "verbatim" — does not exist in any
  repository.** Four places in the code cite it by number. Treat the citation as a forward
  reference to a document that may never have been written, not as something you could go read.
- **Every hostname an install serves — an internal one (e.g. `atlas.example.internal`) and, if the
  install has one, an external one (e.g. `atlas.example.com`) — shares one `Secure`, `__Host-` cookie behaviour** — do not "fix" a login that appears not to work
  on a plain-HTTP path by dropping `Secure`; the fix is always the TLS hostname, never the cookie flag.

**Per-node visibility is ENFORCED, and it is two marks, not one.** An earlier version of this
document called it "built and wired, and currently a no-op everywhere it matters"; that has not
been true since per-account access shipped on 2026-08-16, and it is the second sentence in this
section describing a shipped mechanism as a pending one. `node_visibility` (under its own
SQLAlchemy `Base`, deliberately not the auth one, so a node outlives the pass that might otherwise
cascade-delete its mark) holds `visibility` per node — `private`, `shared`, or `private-splice`
(the third is a schema-only placeholder for an undecided design choice; nothing writes it). One
flag has exactly two outcomes, owner-only or everyone, so it cannot answer *private to whom* —
**`node_grant` is the missing half**, a row meaning "this ACCOUNT may see this PRIVATE node".
`_visible_node_ids(session)` in `app.py` is the sole enforcement point, called inside every read
query as a `WHERE id IN (...)` — never as a filter applied after loading, which would leak a
hidden node's existence through a count even while hiding its row. It returns `None` ("no
restriction") for an owner and, as a fast path, for any caller with nothing left
private-and-ungranted. **That fast path is not the normal state once an install marks anything
private (for example a top-level project node such as `example-project`)**, and an owner administers marks and grants from the board with
the **Access** button in the board's top bar (owner-only; legacy board: Settings → Access & sharing,
`frontend/settings.js`), writing through `PUT /api/access/node/{node_id}`, which costs the `admin`
scope *on top of* the owner role — so an owner's `read`-scoped token is still refused. **Grants inherit person → bot and ROLE NEVER DOES**
(ADR 0034): an owner holds no grants — unrestricted by role, before a grant row is ever read — so
linking an owner's agent to them makes it *less* capable, not more, which is the safety property
and the reason linking is on by default. Where a node is not resolved by mark or grant directly,
`visible(n)` walks `contains` parents recursively, requires **ALL** of them (union semantics would
let a second parent silently un-hide a subtree), and fails **closed** on a cycle or an unresolvable
parent id rather than guessing visible. A workitem carries no mark and has no `contains` parent, so
it follows **what it works on** through the effective binding — found in a browser after the whole
suite had passed.

**Scope enforcement is real now, and it was not until 2026-08-15.** `Principal.has_scope` existed
with zero call sites for weeks; `guard_write` returned "allowed" for every non-session principal
before scope was ever consulted, so a service token minted `--scopes read` could reach
`DELETE /api/node/{id}?cascade=1`. The fix closed it: every non-session principal — a token, and
the dormant `grace` bypass, which had the identical hole — now goes through `_check_write_scope`,
which maps the route's *template* path (`request.scope["route"].path`, not the request's literal
URL, so a key like `{node_id}` matches) and method against `WRITE_SCOPE_ROUTES`, and fails closed:
a mutating route with no entry in that map is refused, never allowed by default. The scope domain
is `read, write, ingest, admin, private`; deleting a node or an edge needs `admin`, everything else
that mutates needs `write`. **Until this shipped, "not issuing the token" was the only real
limiter on a token's blast radius — that sentence is now historical, not current, and anything
still citing it (older notes in the repository did, as of
2026-08-14) is describing a fixed bug as a live one.**

**Two credential kinds, deliberately not three.** `Authorization: Bearer atlas_svc_…` is a
machine; the `__Host-atlas_session` cookie is a human; both present is `400`, refused outright
rather than guessed at. There is no third branch reading an identity header set by an access proxy
in front of Atlas — no such proxy is part of the install and nothing issues such a header on any
path Atlas serves, so the class of bug where a peer forges it does not exist because the code that
would read it is not written.

**And the enforcement is checked structurally, not by sampling.** `verify_node_access.py` §F walks
`app.app.routes` and FAILS the build on any route with no access classification, so an endpoint
added later that forgets the filter cannot ship quietly. §F2 (2026-08-28) applies the
same fail-closed rule one level down: every query PARAMETER of an access-filtered route must appear
in `PARAM_COVERAGE`, classified as selecting node rows or as only shaping the response. It exists
because a route stops being the unit of access review once its parameters decide which rows come
back — `?assignee=` arrived on an already-classified `/api/workitems` and §F stayed green the whole
time.
paragraphs.atlas-signals.abstract|ac44feb25442fc24:
**Nothing here is hand-set.** ADR 0019's rule is that every value is re-derivable from node status
plus edges, so `recompute_derived()` runs in the same unit of work as any write that changes a
status or an edge — and there is no scheduler and no cache left to drift. Since the boot ingest was
deleted, recompute-on-write is the *only* trigger there is.
paragraphs.atlas-signals.detail|7fc07903446833a4:
**What that leaves on the World tab, measured on live (snapshot, date not recorded):** no world node
carried a non-zero `completion` or `attention_count`. Both are `contains`-subtree measures and world
objects have no status, while workitems attach by `works_on`, which no rollup follows. Fill works,
from the hints; ring and badge read empty on every object. The two items once filed against this —
`subtree_work_load()` and the original RAG derivation — are both cancelled, so
nothing is currently scheduled to change it.
paragraphs.atlas-signals.detail|bbe9c61f9b8d6e0d:
**The static hint.** An object-family leaf takes its fill from `attributes.health`, a hand-set
string; missing or unrecognised means grey. Probes are **out of scope by decision** (the owner,
2026-08-10), and this node owns the `probes-and-health-out-of-scope` non-goal that records it: the
`probe` and `probe_result` tables exist, nothing feeds them, and nothing is being built on them.
paragraphs.atlas-signals.detail|bddec4e78837bb33:
**`work_load()` is deliberately not a rollup.** It is a per-object readout over *effective* bindings: a workitem's own `works_on` edge, or the nearest bound ancestor's **in the work
hierarchy, never the world one**. It is computed on read rather than cached and attached to every
node by `/api/graph`, so the panel renders it without a second fetch.
paragraphs.atlas-signals:docs/nodes/atlas-signals/a:
There is **no scheduler**. `recompute_derived` used to be called at the end of the boot ingest as
well; that ingest is deleted, so recompute-on-write is the only trigger. Everything it
writes is a cache of something `derive()` can produce again from status plus edges, which is the
property that makes a stale-colour drift impossible rather than merely unlikely.

So on a world node today: the colour is a hand-set hint rolled up, the ring is empty, and the badge
never appears. The number people actually read on an object comes from `work_load` instead — the
panel's "N workitems · M done (X%)" — and the panel says so in as many words: *"Direct links only —
a rollup over this object's sub-tree isn't computed yet."* That rollup was cancelled; nothing is scheduled to add it.
paragraphs.atlas-tooling.abstract|28ea164541023bc2: It exists as a node because the scripts it holds needed somewhere to bind that wasn't a project root itself — before ADR 0030 gave the tree capability nodes, binding tooling work straight to the `atlas` project root would have turned that root into a shadow backlog. Nothing is deployed here — the scripts run from a workstation or as one-off jobs against the install, and the CLI runs inside `atlas-api`, which is why it carries no `hosted_on` edge.
paragraphs.atlas-tooling:docs/nodes/atlas-tooling/a:
- **CI checks; it does not gate.** The verify suite runs on every push, but nothing blocks a
  merge, and staging, measuring and closing the ticket still depend on someone doing them.
- **A live-facing tool and a test-facing tool look similar and are not interchangeable.**
  `apply_intents.py`/`apply_node_docs.py` need a real `--base` URL and a minted, then revoked,
  Bearer token; `verify_all.py` needs neither — it never touches a deployed database, only a
  disposable one it owns for the run. Pointing the wrong one at the wrong place is an easy typo
  with very different consequences (one writes real rows; the other cannot reach them at all
  without `ATLAS_TEST_DB_URL` deliberately overridden).
- **This node's own summary has been observed to describe deleted machinery** — a prior review of
  this node named "the arrival gate" and "the importers" among its scripts; both were deleted on
  2026-08-12. Treat any inventory of this component that predates that date as
  unverified until re-checked against `tools/` and `backend/verify_*.py` on disk.
- **Re-running `apply_node_docs.py` against a board that has since diverged is not free of
  judgment even though it is free of overwrite risk.** A skip is silent per-field, not per-node —
  a node could get a new `docs[]` entry appended while its already-authored `abstract` is left
  untouched, which is correct but easy to misread as "nothing happened."

**The verify suite finds itself; nothing lists it.** `verify_all.py` discovers every
`backend/verify_*.py` on disk, starts one disposable `postgres:16-alpine` (uuid name, free port,
torn down via `atexit`) that the *run* owns, and executes each script serially against it via
`ATLAS_TEST_DB_URL`. That shape is a direct fix for a real incident: on 2026-08-10 two agents ran
scripts concurrently against one shared container and one dropped the other's schema mid-run, and
both then reported green on a re-run. Two runs now always get two containers, and a script never
silently reports success against a database it could not reach — `backend/testdb.py` has exactly
three outcomes (`ATLAS_TEST_DB_URL` if set, else a disposable container, else a hard failure) and
raises rather than falling back to anything, including SQLite, which is gone from this repo
entirely. Individual scripts still run standalone (`python verify_object_graph.py`)
and behave identically.

- **The verify suite** — `backend/verify_all.py` plus every `verify_*.py` on disk, run by hand and
  by `.github/workflows/verify.yml` on every push and pull request against a disposable Postgres.
- **The install's deploy procedure** — on OpenShift, the install's Kustomize overlay under
  `deploy/openshift/overlays/<name>/`, applied with `oc apply -k` (or rendered by Argo CD); on the
  Compose install, `docker compose up` from the installation's checkout (`docs/oss/INSTALL.md`).
- **The one-off seed appliers** — `tools/seed-intents/` and `tools/seed-node-docs/`, each a small
  Python script plus its authored payload, POSTing to a real Atlas API over HTTP with a minted
  Bearer token.
- **The operator CLI** — `atlas-admin`, shipped in the `atlas-api` image and run inside that
  container on whichever install holds the database being administered:
  `docker compose exec -T atlas-api atlas-admin …`, or on OpenShift
  `oc exec <pod> -c atlas-api -- atlas-admin …`.

**Two scripts have started deriving their expectations from the application's own source of
truth instead of a hand-copied list, and it is worth knowing which**: `verify_object_graph.py`'s
route inventory is built from `auth.WRITE_SCOPE_ROUTES` directly (`set(auth.WRITE_SCOPE_ROUTES)`,
not a second list somebody has to remember to update), and its §20 asserts every one of those
routes actually refuses a read-only Bearer token — the regression test for the exact gap
`atlas-security` describes being closed on 2026-08-15.

**Test data is a curated, self-checking fixture, not a slice of production.** `backend/testseed.py`
inserts ~31 nodes built to contain every case the rules need exactly once, with ids that cannot be
mistaken for real work, then runs `self_check()` to prove each declared case is actually present
after derivation. Before 2026-08-12 several scripts got their data by importing real backlog
markdown instead — which pinned the suite to real ids (an assertion broke when someone closed the
work item it named; one later sweep found six such stale-looking assertions in one script, and the
sixth turned out not to be stale at all, it was a real defect a noisy neighbour had been hiding) and
to one workstation (the server could not clone the planning repository the markdown lived in).
Both couplings are gone with the markdown itself.

**The seed appliers exist to make one-time authoring reviewable, and refuse to become a second
importer.** Both `tools/seed-intents/apply_intents.py` and `tools/seed-node-docs/apply_node_docs.py`
follow the same shape: the judgment (which statement, which prose, which document) lives in a
committed JSON file, reviewed in a diff before anything is sent; the script only ever **creates**.
`apply_intents.py` POSTs and treats a `409` (an existing `(node_id, slug)`) as SKIP; there is no
`--force`. `apply_node_docs.py` checks presence before writing — a node whose `abstract` is already
non-empty is skipped whole, a `docs[]` path that already has content is skipped, and `attributes`
is read-modify-written rather than replaced, because `PATCH /api/node` assigns the whole dict and
sending only `docs[]` would silently drop everything else already on the node. This is a direct,
named reaction to the three markdown importers ADR 0029 retired: they were `setattr`
upserts, so a second run did not top the database up, it reverted it to the file. **The instant
either applier's rows exist in Postgres, the database is authoritative and the source directory is
a historical record — not something to edit and re-run expecting the board to follow.**

**A staging environment, if the install has one, ships a committed tree, never the working
directory** — on OpenShift that holds by construction, because an overlay names its images by tag
and digest, built from a commit — so staging always reflects a real commit. See `atlas-ops` for the
isolation mechanics (namespaces or containers, volumes, network, port).
paragraphs.atlas-visibility.abstract|cb79a68561bd3e: **It is BUILT and live** (2026-08-16). Earlier text here said most of it was specified and not yet built, that nothing wrote to the table, and that `/api/graph` was unfiltered — none of that has been true since per-account access shipped. On a live install, nodes such as an org and a private project can be marked private. An owner administers this with the **Access** button in the board's top bar (owner-only; legacy board: Settings → Access & sharing), accounts down and projects across, and `verify_node_access.py` §F fails the build on any `/api` route with no access classification.
paragraphs.atlas-visibility:docs/nodes/atlas-visibi:
**A route is not the unit of access review once its parameters decide which rows come back.**
`?assignee=` arrived on an already-classified `/api/workitems` and §F stayed green throughout,
which is why §F2 (2026-08-28) classifies every query PARAMETER of every filtered route
as either selecting node rows or only shaping the response, and fails on an unclassified one.

> **Status, 2026-08-28.** This is **live and enforced**. `node_visibility` holds rows on live —
> for example an org node and a private project marked private — and `node_grant` carries the per-account half.
> Every node-reading `/api` route applies the filter *inside the query*, and
> `verify_node_access.py` fails the build on a route (§F) or a query parameter (§F2) that has no
> access classification. The banner here used to say "zero rows", "global enforcement does not
> exist" and "tests that have not been written yet"; all three stopped being true when
> per-account access shipped on 2026-08-16.

`_visible_node_ids` (`backend/app.py`) returns the set of node ids the current principal may
see, or `None` meaning "no restriction". It is fail-closed at every branch. **There is no global
choke point** — the `do_orm_execute`-over-every-`Session` design (ADR 0026) was never
built, and this per-query implementation is what actually refuses. Read that as *one rule applied
at every read call site*, not as a stopgap: because it is per-query, a new route does not inherit
it, and §F of the oracle is what stops somebody forgetting.

| surface | filtered today | note |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /api/node/{id}` | yes | inside the `WHERE`, so hidden and non-existent return the same 404 |
| `GET /api/workitems` | yes | `total` is computed *after* the filter |
| `GET /api/intents` | yes | owner-side rows only |
| `GET /api/graph` | yes | seeds, BFS hops and rollups all filtered (**done** 2026-08-16) |
| `GET /api/graph/tree` | yes | the node dict is filtered and the roots are derived from it |
| the node-document read route | yes | `_may_see_node`, so a doc on a hidden node 404s identically |
| `GET /api/events` | yes | on BOTH governing node columns, before `total` is counted |
| every `Session` globally | **no, and not planned** | the `do_orm_execute` choke point was never built; the rule is applied per query instead, and `verify_node_access.py` §F is what makes that safe |

1. **Utelämnat = oförändrat (AC3).** Ingen rad skrivs, svaret ser ut som i dag, `_visible_node_ids`
   snabbväg ("inget privat") fortsätter att gälla. `"shared"` explicit skriver **ingen** rad —
   delad är frånvaron av märkning, samma princip som `put_access` (`app.py:5866`).
2. **Samma transaktion (AC2).** Raderna läggs till före `recompute_derived(s)`, som är vägens enda
   commit. Alla kontroller av `visibility`/`grants` (okänt värde, okänt konto, otillåtet för rollen)
   körs **innan** noden läggs till och innan ett task-id prägas, så att ett avslag varken lämnar nod,
   rad eller förbrukat id. Ett fel efter `s.add` rullar tillbaka allt (befintligt kontrakt).
3. **Bara åtstramning är fri.** `private` är tillåtet för varje anropare som passerar `guard_write`:
   det kan bara göra noden *mindre* synlig. `grants` till **andra** konton är ägar-only (403, fältet
   namngivet) — det är en vidgning och ska kosta detsamma som i Settings.
4. **Skaparen tappar inte sin egen nod.** En icke-ägare som skapar privat får automatiskt en grant
   till sitt eget konto; en agent dessutom till sin person (`person_user_id`, ADR 0034). Utan detta
   skapar en medlem en nod som omedelbart 404:ar för hen själv. En ägare får ingen auto-grant (roll
   räcker) — men en ägares **agent** får en grant till sitt eget konto, eftersom ägaren inte har några
   grants att ärva.
5. **`private-splice` avvisas vid skapande** (400 `unknown_visibility`): dess betydelse är inte
   beslutad.
6. **`shared` under privat förälder avtäcker ingenting.** ALL-föräldrar-regeln gäller oförändrad;
   svaret får ett additivt fält `effective_visibility` så att anroparen ser att noden ärver privat —
   **bara när `visibility` eller `grants` skickades**, så att ett anrop utan fälten får ett
   byte-identiskt svar.
7. **Granskning.** Samma `auth_event` (`node_visibility_changed`, `node_grant_added`) som `put_access`
   skriver, via en utbruten hjälpare — inte en andra implementation. Aldrig `graph_event`
   (samma skäl som vid `app.py:5900`).
8. **Synlighet ändras aldrig via patch.** `atlas_node_write` mot en *befintlig* nod med `visibility`
   eller `grants` avvisas lokalt (`visibility_on_existing_node`) och pekar på Settings. Det bevarar
   motiveringen vid `app.py:5600`: att ett namnbyte inte ska kunna dela om ett projekt.

> **Flyttat hit 2026-11-10** från en aldrig committad fil, `docs/proposals/create-time-visibility.md` i repot.
> Fil:rad-hänvisningarna gäller en äldre version (2026-10-21), då backend låg i `app.py`. Backend är sedan dess uppdelad i
> `backend/routers/`, så raderna stämmer inte längre. Förslaget var inte genomfört 2026-11-10: `NodeWrite` i
> `backend/routers/nodes.py` har inga fält för synlighet. Det bifogade `impl-plan.md` och ADR-utkastet följde inte med.
paragraphs.atlas-work-store.detail|0537d5cef96a359e:
- **Assignment is NOT a grant.** The reference never enters `_visible_node_ids`. A workitem bound to a private project and assigned to an account with no grant on it is absent from every route for that account — **their own `?assignee=me` included**. `verify_assignment.py` proves it by breaking it rather than asserting the happy path.
- **Reading it.** `GET /api/people` returns `{id, username, name}` and nothing else; `?for=<workitem-id>` narrows to accounts that can SEE that item. `GET /api/workitems?assignee=<id|me|none>`, with `?include_ancestors=1` for the root-first, access-filtered `contains` chain per row.
- **Agents are not assignable** (ADR 0034) — enforced in `routers/workitems._resolve_assignee` with a 400 naming the field. The picker merely declines to offer them. The MCP tools cannot set an assignee at all; handing work over goes through the HTTP API or the board.
- **Any signed-in account may view any other account's Mine list.** Deliberate: *"if all can see all thats great for now"* (the owner, 2026-08-18). Narrowing it was considered and set aside.
paragraphs.atlas-work-store.detail|0ae083b60058cbb0: **A workitem has no priority field.** The WSJF-style score in `routers/legacy_v0.compute_priority` (`value`, `effort`, `urgency`, `risk`) belongs to world components, not to workitems, so `POST`/`PATCH /api/workitem` accept a `priority` key and store nothing, and the board offers no control for it. Urgency is carried in the name instead, as a `CRITICAL:` prefix.
paragraphs.atlas-work-store.detail|924902381a948140:
- **What may be written is `attention.SETTABLE_STATUSES`:** `pending`, `analyze`, `in_progress`, `blocked`, `done`, `cancelled`. `analyze` is a real in-flight status. **`cancelled` is a second terminal status, treated the same as `done`** (the owner, 2026-08-10: *"cancelled should be treated as the same as complete"*).
- **`STATUS_EQUIVALENT`** beside it maps authored synonyms (`planned`, `todo`, `wip`, …) onto a settable status, and is **mirrored in `frontend/state.js` — keep the two equal**. It is why a `planned` task lights the `pending` button instead of showing nothing selected.
- **Status has one branch for every node** since `status_override` and the three-way merge were deleted: normalise, validate, write `attributes["status"]`, recompute. Read effective status through `attention.status_map()`, never `attributes["status"]` directly.
paragraphs.atlas-work-store:docs/nodes/atlas-work-s:
Comments follow the same rule for the same reason: a conversation in its own table cannot be lost to
a `body` rewrite. And nothing a comment said is lost to its own edit or delete either (the owner,
2026-10-29, auditability): a delete hides the row, and an edit keeps the replaced text in
`workitem_comment_revision`. The one path that removes them is deleting the whole item
(`DELETE /api/node/{id}?cascade=1`, admin), which `_delete_node_dependents` does for every side table.

`PATCH /api/workitem` assigns `body` wholesale. Anything living inside `body` is therefore destroyed
by any edit that does not carefully reproduce it, and that is not hypothetical: recording outcomes
on three tasks cost 3,291 / 2,513 / 2,170 characters, recoverable then only because the
markdown still existed. Splitting acceptance and result into their own rows makes that class of loss
**structurally impossible** rather than merely discouraged. All 7,974 characters were reconciled
before the files were deleted.
paragraphs.atlas-world-model.abstract|11cd6e1a47df1:
`contains` is "is part of", the product decomposition and nothing else. `works_on` binds a workitem to at most one world object. `depends_on` orders workitems against each other. `hosted_on` says where a service or database actually *runs*, as opposed to what it is *part of*. `instance_of` points a deployment at what it deploys, instead of forking the tree beside it. `contributes_to` is a person or org contributing to a project, many-to-many. `uses` is one project standing on another without owning it. `requires` (ADR 0044) is a hard run-time dependency between world objects — A does not work without B — and is the edge an impact question walks; it is its own type because `depends_on` stays workitem-only, read by the blocked-work signals with no family filter.
- **Node granularity is a judgment call, not a fixed count.** ADR 0030 originally targeted 5-25 open workitems per node; the owner retired that ceiling on 2026-08-15 once a legitimately busy node crossed it doing nothing wrong — a node acquires work because work exists, not because it became hard to read. Split a node when finding its work actually gets hard, not when a count crosses a line. The one piece of the old reasoning that still stands: count **open** work, never lifetime — a lifetime count only rises, so a threshold on it would fire everywhere eventually just from work being finished.
- **The outlives-the-work test.** If it is finished when the epic is finished, it is an epic, not a node.
paragraphs.atlas-world-model.abstract|1bc145e644edc:
- **Three families**, carried on `node_type.family`. `workitem` (epic, story, task), `object` (org, project, system, service, component, agent, db, host, capability) and `bridge` (skill, vision; `doc` is retired vocabulary still seeded in `BRIDGE_TYPES`, `goal` is removed). The family, not the type, is what read filters and edge rules key on.
- **Roots are derived, and there is no owner above them.** A root is "a node with no incoming `contains`", never listed. ADR 0030 set the original install's roots: `atlas` and a few other projects, plus one org. A project added since without a parent is a root too. `GET /api/graph/tree` gives the live list, not this sentence. Ownership is an edge, not a position in the tree, so a rendering anchor above the roots is a layout device and must never be visible.
- **The edge vocabulary lives in the `edge_type` TABLE**, not in this paragraph — one row per type carrying its legal `(src_family, dst_family)` pairs, its meaning, and whether it is `active` or `dead`. What follows is the human summary of the *active* ones and is not the authority; `serves` and `for` are also declared, both `dead`, and drift between this vocabulary and what the graph actually holds is reported on `/api/health`. See `detail`.

- **Board content must suit everyone the board is shown to.** The board is visible to every invitee, and the privacy notice at `/auth/privacy` (`auth._privacy_page`) is written on that assumption.

paragraphs.atlas-world-model.detail|b32f21be42c6ce8: **Wiring enforcement to the registry was built, measured and DECLINED** (the owner, 2026-08-27) — the reasoning is written beside `EDGE_FAMILY_RULES` in `deps.py`, and the implementation is preserved on branch `feat/edge-type-registry-followup`. Two reasons: reading `pairs` as *permission* rather than *description* would make a work-hierarchy `contains` edge creatable through the generic endpoint, and therefore through `atlas_edge_write` by every federated MCP client — a route that does not REPLACE an existing parent the way `POST /api/workitem` does, so a task could quietly acquire a second parent. And the gap is small: the drift check already observes the hazard, and live carries zero `serves` and zero `for`. **If it is ever revisited, separate the two questions first**: `pairs` answers what combinations legitimately EXIST, not what may be CREATED here, and the table cannot currently tell them apart.
paragraphs.atlas-world-model.detail|b7c8eef4e8da911: ADR 0032 (in the installation's ADR registry) is the authority — the union-over-parents rule, slug shadowing as the only override, and the four kinds (`constraint` a bug when violated, `principle` a defect, `non-goal` a removal, `outcome` direction with no work) with what each obliges an agent to DO. **Work rolls UP; intent rolls DOWN**, and that is not a contradiction of ADR 0028: work is a quantity, and rolling it down double-counts; intent is a constraint, and a constraint on the whole binds the part.
paragraphs.atlas-world-model.detail|fdf9d31b06699e8: `pairs` is a LIST per type, which the most-used row is the reason for: `contains` legitimately carries `object → object` (the world hierarchy), `workitem → workitem` (the work hierarchy) **and `object → bridge`**. **The world and work hierarchies share the one `contains` string permanently**: giving the work side its own `decomposes_into` type was cancelled on 2026-08-27 together with its story, so a `contains` walk from a world node falls straight through an epic into every story and task beneath it unless it is scoped with `families=object`. The `object → bridge` pair was missing from the first seed and live found it within a day: a capability node contained a skill node, and `skill` was the only bridge-family node with any rows at all. The vocabulary as written down — here, in `AGENTS.md` and in `EDGE_FAMILY_RULES` — had been incomplete against reality and nobody knew.

- **`host.docker.internal:<port>`** — the pattern sibling MCP servers on one host often use — cannot
  work when `atlas-api` publishes on `127.0.0.1` only. From inside a container that name resolves to
  the host's bridge address, not its loopback, so the connection is refused.
- **`https://atlas-api:8443`** over a shared network fails differently, and would fail even if the
  networks were joined: the gate checks the `Host` header against an allow-list *before any handler
  runs* and answers **421** to anything not on it. `ATLAS_INTERNAL_HOSTS` is the one setting that
  admits a Bearer request on an internal name, and the OSS installs set it to the TLS front's
  internal door only (`atlas-api:9443` in Compose, `atlas-tls.<namespace>.svc:9443` on OpenShift),
  never to atlas-api's own name.

There is deliberately **no ingest**: boot being a read is what lets Atlas own its own data. Backups
are the install's decision, not a default — an install may decide to run without them and accept
that losing the database means losing the work, and should record that as an intent on this node if
it does. In Compose they are opt-in (`atlas-admin backup`, and the `backup` compose profile), off
unless asked for. On OpenShift the `cnpg` component takes **no backup**; the
`cnpg-objectstore-plugin` component adds WAL archiving and a daily `ScheduledBackup` to object
storage, and a backup taken by hand before each migrate Job is the documented habit. A one-off
recovery point taken before a bounded experiment is not a backup, and is never scheduled as one.

paragraphs.atlas:docs/nodes/atlas/architecture.md|2:
- **The gateway authorizes per ROUTE, not per caller.** Every call to `atlas-mcp` carries the
  caller's own `Authorization: Bearer`, which atlas-api checks, so a caller sees and writes as
  itself; there is no shared MCP token. But a tool
  federated through an MCP gateway is offered to every client of the route, and only atlas-api's
  token check tells callers apart — which is why `atlas_delete` is never federated.
- **`/assets/*.js` carry no cache-busting in the URL** — `/assets/panel.js`, never
  `panel.abc123.js`. Since 2026-08-18 that no longer strands an open tab on last week's code: every
  asset ships `Cache-Control: private, no-cache`, so the browser may store a copy but must
  revalidate, and an unchanged file costs a 304. The residual hazard is narrower and lives at an
  edge, if the install has one — a copy a CDN or caching edge in front of Atlas already holds lives
  out its TTL, so that host can serve a stale module after the internal host is already correct.
  Confirm what the container holds before believing the browser, and check every host that serves
  the board, not only the internal one.
- **The board's D3 positions cannot be measured from a backgrounded tab** — transitions never advance
  and every node reports the origin. Counts, computed styles and panel text are reliable; layout is not.
- **`node.name` carries two registers.** Prose names a concept for a human; identifier is the exact
  string the thing answers to elsewhere. Rendering must stay verbatim — an uppercase-first transform
  would corrupt every identifier and make the map disagree with the API.
- **Work rolls up, intent rolls down.** Not a contradiction: work is a quantity and rolling it down
  would double-count; intent is a constraint, and a constraint on the whole binding the part is what
  `contains` asserts.

One repo per world root (ADR 0031), so Atlas's code, decisions and deploy notes are all in the
installation's repository. Nothing about Atlas lives in another repository except the few ADRs that
bind more than one root.

| | what it is | how it is reached |
|---|---|---|
| `atlas-api` | the whole backend: FastAPI, serves the board too | never directly from outside: TLS on `:8443`, reached only through the TLS front `atlas-tls` (on OpenShift, Service `atlas-api` inside the namespace) |
| database | every durable byte | no published port: `atlas-postgres` on the Compose network, or on OpenShift the CloudNativePG cluster `atlas-db`, TLS required |
| reverse proxy (`atlas-tls`) | TLS terminator in front of atlas-api and atlas-mcp | `:8443`; on OpenShift behind the Route, which re-encrypts to it and is the only way in from outside the cluster |
| tunnel connector (optional) | public transport, only if an install chooses to publish one | no inbound port at all — the connector dials out |
| `atlas-mcp` | the agent tool surface | `https://atlas.example.internal/mcp/` through the front door; itself TLS on `:8493`, no published port |
| an MCP gateway (optional) | federates several MCP servers behind one endpoint | its own TLS door (the Compose `gateway` profile publishes `:8444`); never a plain-HTTP route to atlas-mcp |
| GitHub (external, optional) | "Sign in with GitHub" and collaborator invitations to ONE repo; off unless turned on | outbound HTTPS from `atlas-api` only; nothing at GitHub calls in except the browser's OAuth redirect back |

- **Tracked, in git.** The compose file in `deploy/oss/`, or on OpenShift the Kustomize base plus the
  install's own overlay, kept in the organisation's own repository and pointing at the base by
  release tag. The overlay's settings say, among other things, where atlas-mcp finds atlas-api
  (`ATLAS_BASE_URL`). Keep the configuration the running install actually uses under version
  control, so any change to it shows as a diff: a configuration file that lives outside git can be
  rewritten by a session and silently drop settings, and nothing looks wrong because health stays
  green.
- **Secret, never in git.** The two peppers and the database credentials are files: in Compose under
  `deploy/oss/secrets/`, on OpenShift Secrets (`atlas-peppers`, the CloudNativePG app Secret)
  mounted read-only, with `ATLAS_REQUIRE_SECRET_FILES=1` refusing the plain forms. atlas-mcp holds no
  token of its own — each tool call forwards its caller's Bearer token — and reads `ATLAS_TOKEN` only
  under the opt-in shared-token fallback. **The peppers cannot be regenerated** — they are mixed into
  every stored password verifier and token digest, so changing one invalidates every account and
  every token at once. **The GitHub credentials, if GitHub linking is turned on, are three files**
  (`oauth_client_id`, `oauth_client_secret`, `invite_token`), read through the
  `ATLAS_GITHUB_*_FILE` settings from `<secrets-dir>/github/`, owner-only and mounted read-only.
- **Outside Atlas's configuration altogether.** Configuration for services outside Atlas — for
  example an MCP gateway's config file — lives with those services. Keep any runtime-state directory
  gitignored deliberately, so it cannot be committed wholesale by accident.

**GitHub is the one external service `atlas-api` calls for identity.** It does two things there:
exchanges an OAuth code to learn which GitHub account a signed-in person owns (the user token is
used once and dropped), and, when the owner ticks *repo access*, invites or removes that account as a
collaborator on the one repository named by `ATLAS_GITHUB_REPO` (for example
`example-org/example-repo`) with a fine-grained token. The flow and its rules are on
`atlas-identity` → *GitHub link and repo access*. The feature is off unless the install turns it on (`github_link` is in the OSS default

offers OIDC sign-in (`ATLAS_AUTH_PROVIDERS`) calls its identity provider.

The detour in that diagram is real and is the thing people trip over: **`atlas-mcp` never talks to
`atlas-api` directly — it goes back in through the TLS front, `atlas-tls`**. In Compose atlas-mcp
calls `https://atlas-api:9443`, a front of `atlas-tls` that is published nowhere; on OpenShift it

paragraphs.atlas:docs/nodes/atlas/architecture.md|e:
**Configuration splits three ways, and the split is the thing to learn.** In Compose it all sits under
`deploy/oss/`, with secrets as files in its `./secrets/`; on OpenShift it sits in the install's own
overlay, with secrets as Secret objects mounted as files:

Where the services sit decides how they reach each other. A single-host Docker Compose install that
grew service by service may run every service as its **own compose project on its own network**,
sharing one network only with what it must; everything else — an MCP gateway, other MCP servers —
then communicates through **published host ports**. The OSS installs keep Atlas's own parts
together instead: one compose project in `deploy/oss/`, or one namespace on OpenShift, where the
NetworkPolicies (on by default) decide which pod may reach which port.

paragraphs.panel-docs.detail|2fcde514c58a529e: **Read-only.** The tab renders documents; it does not author them. `PUT` and `DELETE /api/node/{id}/doc` exist (the authoring half of ADR 0029) but nothing in this tab calls them, and *publishing* a stored document stays a separate visible act — a PATCH on the node's `attributes`. `PUT` reports `served: false` with an `expected-not-served` note when the allowlist entry is missing, which is how that state is meant to be discovered.
paragraphs.panel-docs:docs/nodes/panel-docs/archite:
**Three distinguishable outcomes for one path, not two.** An entry marked `external: true`
answers `200` with `{external: true}` and no content — deliberately distinguishable from the 404
an unlisted path gets, so the board can render *"External reference — kept in git, not served
here"* instead of a convincing blank document. A path with no `node_doc` row at all, despite being
listed, is a genuine 404 with a distinct error string. And **"stored but not served" is a real,
expected state** — `PUT /api/node/{id}/doc` (the authoring route) does not require a
`docs[]` entry to exist first, so content can sit in `node_doc` with `GET` 404ing it until someone
adds the allowlist entry as a separate, visible act (a `PATCH` on `attributes`). Storing and
publishing are deliberately two acts, not one.
paragraphs.panel-overview.abstract|fe9a0eea4d1d8a45:
- **For work** (*This item*): status, assignee, priority, labels, *Works on* (the one `works_on` binding, ADR 0028, or the one inherited from the epic), epic, story, parent (a move) and finished date. Changing an existing binding is not supported on board v2 yet; remove it first. Status goes through `POST /api/node/{id}/status`; the rest through `PATCH /api/workitem`. The description (`body`) and the acceptance list are edited in place. A pending acceptance proposal from an agent shows as a diff with **Approve** / **Reject**, which work only from a person's session, and the last attested change is named. Result shows under its own heading (`result_heading`).
- **For a project**: its task-id key, read-only.
- **For any node with work below it**: tiles (done %, active, blocked, need attention), a stacked bar, and a link to the open items on the work board.
- **Description**: a world node's `abstract`, with `detail` under *More*; a workitem's `body`.
- **Documentation**: one link per `docs[]` entry, opening it on the Docs tab.
- **Context** (world nodes): its containers up to a root, the types it contains, and attached skills.
paragraphs.panel-overview:docs/nodes/panel-overview:
Sections append to `tabBodies.overview` in a fixed, deliberate order — *what is this* → *how do we
know it's done* → *what actually happened* (the owner, 2026-08-10):

- **A re-bind is two writes.** `PATCH /api/workitem` refuses a binding onto an item that already
  has one — 409 `binding_exists`, at most one binding per item (ADR 0028) — so *changing* a binding
  sends `binding: null` and then `binding: <new>`. If the second write fails the item would be left
  unbound, a change nobody asked for, so the control restores the previous binding, and if even the
  restore fails it says so on screen. The restore leg deliberately does **not** call `refreshGraph`,
  because the refresh re-renders the panel and would take the error message down with it.
- **A stale label survives in the status control.** `renderStatusSection`'s note under the status
  buttons still reads *"From the backlog file"* (plus `node.source` if present). There has been no
  backlog file since the markdown was deleted on 2026-08-12 — every workitem is
  `atlas`-origin and every status write goes straight to Postgres through the API. This is stale
  UI copy, not a stale fact about the system; it should say something like "via the API," not
  point at a file that no longer exists.
- **The empty-section rule is per-section, not per-tab.** Acceptance and Result vanish
  independently; a workitem with acceptance criteria but no result shows one section, not neither
  and not both-with-one-blank.
- **`fetchFull`'s cache is keyed on node id alone, not on a request generation.** Two renders of
  the *same* node in quick succession (a rapid re-click, or a status write immediately followed by
  a second one) share whichever promise was in flight at cache-set time; this has not been
  observed to misbehave, but nothing here guards against a genuine race the way the write controls'
  own disable-while-pending does.

1. **Intent strip** (ADR 0032) — titles only, above everything else; a node with no intent of its
   own usually still inherits one down `contains`, so this section hides entirely rather than
   print a false empty state, and its count feeds the Intent tab's badge once it resolves.
2. **Status control** (`renderStatusSection`) — **workitems only** (`WORKITEM_TYPES` = epic,
   story, task; `isObject(node)` covers object *and* bridge families and gets neither this nor
   Acceptance/Result). It `POST`s `/api/node/{id}/status` with the CSRF token from `GET /api/me`,
   and on success copies every field of the response onto the same node object the glyph and
   readouts are drawn from — so the panel updates without a reload — then calls
   `hooks.refreshGraph(node.id)`, because a status change moves rollups that live on *other* nodes
   (ancestors, the blocking frontier, the age filter) that this one render cannot see.
   `statusBucket`/`STATUS_EQUIVALENT` map authored synonyms (`planned`, `wip`, `accepted`, …) onto
   the six settable buttons, so an existing status from before the six-value vocabulary lights the
   nearest button instead of showing nothing selected.
3. **Assignee control** (`renderAssigneeSection`) — workitems only. `PATCH /api/workitem` with an
   `auth_user.id` or `null`; the roster is `GET /api/people?for=<id>`, narrowed to accounts that can
   actually SEE this item. Assignment is not a grant, so an account that cannot see the item is not
   offered.
4. **Binding control** (`renderBindingSection`, shipped 2026-08-28) — workitems only. `PATCH
   /api/workitem` with a world-node id or `null`; the candidate roster is derived from
   `GET /api/vocabulary` + `GET /api/graph/tree` and filtered to the **object** family, because
   `works_on` is a (workitem → object) family edge and offering anything else earns a 409
   `family_mismatch`. No node id is written into the file.
5. **Completion bar** — `node.completion_counts` (done/in-progress/todo) if the tree payload
   carries it, else a single-fraction fallback from `node.completion`.
6. **Description** — `node.abstract`, with `node.detail` behind a `More` disclosure, and, for a
   workitem, an in-place editor that `PATCH`es `node.body` wholesale. Renders *"No description
   authored yet"* when `abstract` is empty, never a blank section.
7. **Documentation** — a pointer, not a viewer (the owner, 2026-08-16): one button per `docs[]` entry
   that switches to the Docs tab and opens that document. Overview is a summary; the write-up lives
   on Docs, and nothing on screen used to say so.
8. **Acceptance**, then **Result** — workitems only, each fetched via `fetchFull` and each
   **removing its own section** rather than leaving a header over nothing when the list/text comes
   back empty. Acceptance is editable in place; Result's heading is read from the payload
   (`result_heading`) rather than hardcoded, because a few workitems' source documents used
   `## Outcome` instead.
paragraphs.panel-work.abstract|7012fb3a10df1b96: **ADR 0028's three buckets are not a shape this node is heading for — they are a shape nobody is heading for, by decision.** That ADR decided `own`, `below` and `linked`, rolling **UP** over `contains` and never down (an earlier draft's fourth `above` bucket, pushing an ancestor's work onto every descendant, was rejected by the owner on 2026-08-08), and the invariant stands: *if a node's board shows a containment-derived item, that node's numbers count it.* But the endpoint that would have served the buckets, `GET /api/node/{id}/backlog`, was **cancelled together with its story on 2026-08-28**, together with the panel dashboard and its backlog widget that were its only consumer. The reasoning, recorded on the story: a workitem already shows its full decomposition through its children, so the remaining gap is one world object showing work bound straight to it rather than to the capabilities inside it — narrow, cosmetic, and on a surface that is rarely the one being read. **The gap is admitted in the UI and deliberately unowned.** Reviving it needs someone actually wanting to stand on a project or component node and read everything beneath it as a routine act.
paragraphs.panel-work.detail|0f2a378ab164d6aa: **Two counting rules for whoever ever builds a subtree rollup here.** First, `work_load` counts **effective** bindings: a workitem with no `works_on` of its own counts against its nearest bound ancestor in the work hierarchy, so an unbound item filed tomorrow is not invisible. Second, the world graph is multi-root and a node may have several `contains` parents — `max` rollups (health, attention) are idempotent and safe, but any `sum` rollup must collect a **set** of reachable ids or a node reachable by two paths is counted twice.
paragraphs.panel-work:docs/nodes/panel-work/archite:
**Counting rule that will surprise anyone who does revive `below`:** the world graph is
multi-root, and a node may legitimately have several `contains` parents. `attention.work_load`
(and every `max` rollup like health/attention) is idempotent under that — visiting a node twice
changes nothing. A `sum` rollup is not: it must collect a **set** of reachable ids before counting,
or a node reachable by two paths gets counted twice. `own` (a direct edge count) cannot double
count today because there is nothing to sum across. The cancellation note on the endpoint kept two more:
apply `_visible_node_ids` INSIDE the query rather than as a post-filter, because a post-filter
strips rows and still leaks counts; and count with `NOT EXISTS` rather than a `LEFT JOIN` against
`edge`, because the join multiplies an item by its binding edges.

**That gap is now admitted and unowned, rather than pending.** ADR 0028 settled three buckets —
`own` (bound directly), `below` (bound to something this node contains), `linked` (bound elsewhere
but related) — rolling **up** over `contains` and never down; an earlier draft's fourth `above`
bucket, pushing an ancestor's work onto every descendant, was rejected by the owner on 2026-08-08. Only
`own` was ever built, as counts and a flat list. `GET /api/node/{id}/backlog`, the endpoint that
would have served the fuller picture, does not exist in `backend/app.py` and **is not going to**:
the task and its story were cancelled on 2026-08-28, after
the panel-dashboard story and the backlog widget that were its only consumer were cancelled the
same day. The recorded reasoning is worth carrying, because it is the argument anyone reviving this
has to beat: the *"direct links only"* note fires only for world objects, since a workitem renders
its children and therefore already shows its full decomposition — so what is missing is standing on
a component such as `atlas-frontend` and seeing work bound to the capabilities inside it rather than
to the component itself. Narrow, cosmetic, and on a surface that is rarely the one being read.
Treat ADR 0028 as the decided *model* of how work rolls up, not as a backlog of UI still to build.

**`work_load` is a direct-edge rollup, not a subtree rollup, and the tab says so on screen.**
`attention.work_load` counts only `works_on` edges that land on *this* node — after resolving each
workitem's **effective** binding (a workitem with no `works_on` of its own inherits its
nearest bound ancestor's binding, walking the *work* hierarchy, never the world one). It does not
walk `node.children` to add up what is bound to something this node contains, and the panel is
explicit about the gap: *"Direct links only — a rollup over this object's sub-tree isn't computed
yet."* Re-deriving that client-side would duplicate backend logic over a tree the board has
already pruned by the age filter and the detail slider, and the two numbers would drift with
neither side able to say which one lied — so it deliberately does not try.

atlas-identity:token-belongs-to-the-huma.statement: A service token belongs to an agent's OWN account, and that account records the person accountable for it. Both halves matter, and collapsing them into one sentence has put a false premise into planning before: "belongs to the human" is a claim about ACCOUNTABILITY, never about identity. `admin bot add` creates a distinct `auth_user` per agent and refuses a person outright; `auth.py` refuses any Bearer token whose owning account is not `is_service`. Since ADR 0034, `auth_user.person_user_id` records who is answerable, grants inherit from person to bot, ROLE never does, and disabling a person disables their agents. An owner holds no grants, so an owner's agent inherits an EMPTY set — linking makes it less capable, not more. Two independent bounds apply to every machine caller: scopes bound what it may DO (enforced since 2026-08-15 for every non-session principal, an unmapped route failing closed), and grants bound what it may SEE. Neither removes the accountability of the person who minted it.

atlas-work-store:keep-the-id-scheme|fc77.statement: Slug ids for epics and stories (`EPIC-<slug>`, `STORY-<slug>`), numbers for tasks (`TASK-<n>`). Flattening them, into `EPIC-<n>` numbers or a type-free `ID-XXXXX`, was considered and rejected. No code parses the prefix (type comes from the `type` column), so unifying simplifies nothing and costs legibility in every edge dump, log line and commit. The split matches lifespan: tasks are numerous and disposable, stories and epics are referred to in prose for months. Reopen only if reclassifying a task as a story, or the reverse, becomes common.
